questions.q: Write the augmented matrix for the system $2x+y-z=3$, $x-3y+2z=-1$, $4x+y+z=5$ (give it as its three rows).
questions.answer: Row 1: $\langle2,1,-1,3\rangle$. Row 2: $\langle1,-3,2,-1\rangle$. Row 3: $\langle4,1,1,5\rangle$ (each row lists the $x,y,z$ coefficients, then the right-hand side).

questions.q: List the three types of elementary row operations.
questions.answer: 1. Swap two rows. 2. Multiply a row by a nonzero scalar. 3. Add a multiple of one row to another row.
From the second equation, $x=1+y$. Substituting: $2(1+y)+3y=7 \Rightarrow 5y=5 \Rightarrow y=1$, so $x=2$. Solution: $(2,1)$.
From the second equation, $y=11-5x$. Substituting: $3x-2(11-5x)=4 \Rightarrow 13x=26 \Rightarrow x=2$, so $y=1$. Solution: $(2,1)$.

From the first equation, $x=6-y-z$. Substituting into the third: $2(6-y-z)+5y-z=27 \Rightarrow 3y-3z=15 \Rightarrow y=5+z$. Substituting into the second: $2(5+z)+5z=-4 \Rightarrow 7z=-14 \Rightarrow z=-2$, so $y=3$ and $x=6-3-(-2)=5$. Solution: $(5,3,-2)$.

sections.heading: Why row operations preserve the solution set

questions.q: Explain briefly why multiplying a row by a nonzero constant $c$ doesn't change a system's solution set.
questions.answer: Multiplying both sides of an equation by a nonzero $c$ produces an equivalent equation, since the operation is invertible — dividing by $c$ recovers the original equation exactly.

questions.q: Why is the restriction $c\ne0$ needed for this row operation?
questions.answer: If $c=0$, the row becomes the zero row, which is not invertible — the original row's information is destroyed, so the resulting system need not have the same solution set as the original.
